identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Brihadeeswarar Temple is the Chola imperial temple that Rajaraja I inaugurated in his nineteenth regnal year and named Rajarajesvaram after himself. Devotees revere it as a living Shaiva sanctuary built around one of the largest monolithic Shiva lingas in India, standing about 8.7 m high within the sanctum. Worship established here a thousand years ago has continued without a break, which is why UNESCO's inscription classes it among the 'Great Living Chola Temples'.
sacredClassifications: UNESCO World Heritage Site — Great Living Chola Temples (inscribed 1987)

governance.establishedEra: Early 11th century CE. HR&CE states it was built by Rajaraja I from AD 1003-1010; ASI records that the king inaugurated it in his 19th regnal year, AD 1009-10.

narrative.documentedHistory:
The temple is the principal foundation of the Chola emperor Rajaraja I. The Archaeological Survey of India records that Rajaraja (AD 985-1012) inaugurated it in his nineteenth regnal year, AD 1009-10, and that he named it after himself; the HR&CE Department states that it was built from AD 1003 to 1010. A later inscription referring to the deity as 'Periya Udaiya Nayanar' is the origin of the modern Tamil name Peruvudaiyar Kovil, alongside the Sanskrit-derived Brihadisvara.

The temple stands within a walled inner prakara that ASI measures at 240.9 m east-west by 122 m north-south. The sanctum houses a brihad-linga about 8.7 m high, among the largest monolithic lingas in India. The vimana rises above it in a series of tapering storeys to a height given by secondary sources as 63.4 m, and is crowned by an octagonal cupolic sikhara that rests on a single block of granite — a square of 7.8 m weighing some 80 tons.

The monolithic Nandi facing the sanctum is recorded as weighing about 25 tonnes and measuring 3.65 m high, 5.94 m long and 2.59 m broad. Chola-period mural paintings survive on the walls of the lower ambulatory inside the sanctum wall, which ASI describes as among the finest examples of Chola and later painting.

The Brihadisvara Temple was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1987 as part of the Great Living Chola Temples, a serial property that also includes the Brihadisvara Temple at Gangaikondacholapuram and the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram. It is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India while daily worship continues under the HR&CE Department.
narrative.inscriptionsSummary: ASI records that the moulded plinth of the temple is extensively engraved with inscriptions by its royal builder, in which Rajaraja refers to his many endowments and pious acts.
